questions.q: What is an atlas?
questions.a: An atlas is a book or collection of maps.
o: A book or collection of maps
A sphere on which a map is drawn
A map that shows only mountains, oceans and rivers
A set of map symbols fixed by the Survey of India

questions.q: On a town map, the arrow marked N points to the top of the page. Arjun walks from the post office to the bus stand, which is drawn straight below the post office. He then walks to the park, which is drawn straight to the left of the bus stand. In which direction is the park from the post office?
questions.a: Southwest: the bus stand is south of the post office and the park is west of the bus stand, so the park lies to the southwest of the post office.

questions.q: A village map uses the scale 1 cm = 50 m. On the map, the well is 6 cm from the temple. How far apart are they on the ground?
questions.a: 300 m, because 6 x 50 m = 300 m.

questions.q:
Match each line from a map in Column A with what it shows in Column B.
Column A:
1. The road to the fort is 4 cm long on the map, and 1 cm stands for 2 km.
2. The lake is to the northeast of the fort.
3. A small sign marks every post office.
4. The map shows all the States of India and their capitals.
Column B:
A. symbols
B. direction
C. a political map
D. distance (scale)
(a) Name the three important components of a map. (b) Which of these lets you work out how far apart two places really are on the ground?
questions.a: (a) Distance, direction and symbols. (b) Distance, shown by the map's scale.

questions.q: True or False? 'All countries use the same set of map symbols.' Give the verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Different countries use different sets of symbols. In India, the Survey of India, a government body, has fixed a set of symbols for maps of India.
s: Corrects it: different countries use different sets; the Survey of India has fixed the set for maps of India

questions.q: (a) Name the four cardinal directions, starting from north and moving clockwise. (b) Write the intermediate direction that lies between south and west. (c) On most maps, what single sign shows the directions?
questions.a: (a) North, east, south, west. (b) Southwest (SW). (c) An arrow marked with the letter N, which points to the north.
s: (a) North, east, south, west in clockwise order
(c) An arrow marked N pointing north

questions.q: A district map has the scale 1 cm = 2 km. On it, the hospital is drawn 3.5 cm from the bus stand and the college is drawn 4 cm from the bus stand. (a) What is the real distance from the bus stand to the hospital? (b) What is the real distance from the bus stand to the college? (c) The district is redrawn on a bigger chart with the scale 1 cm = 1 km. How long will the line from the bus stand to the college be on the new chart?
questions.a: (a) 3.5 x 2 km = 7 km. (b) 4 x 2 km = 8 km. (c) The real distance is still 8 km, and 1 cm now stands for 1 km, so the line is 8 cm long.
s: (c) Uses the real distance of 8 km with the new scale to get 8 cm

questions.q:
Students of a school in Shillong draw a map of their locality for a project.
(a) What is a map?
(b) They also want a map that mainly shows the hills and streams of the locality. Which type of map is this?
(c) Their map has the scale 1 cm = 100 m, and the market is drawn 7 cm from the school. What is the real distance between them?
(d) The market is to the northeast of the school. In which direction is the school from the market?
(e) Why do they mark the post office and the police station with symbols instead of drawing each building?
questions.a: (a) A map is a representation, or drawing, of an area as if viewed from the top. (b) A physical map, which mainly shows natural features. (c) 7 x 100 m = 700 m. (d) Southwest, the opposite of northeast. (e) There is not enough space on a map to draw every building; symbols let many details be shown in the limited space.
s: (a) A drawing or representation of an area viewed from the top
(e) Symbols save space so many details fit on the map

questions.q:
A trekking club in Uttarakhand has two maps of the same valley. Map P has the scale 1 cm = 5 km and shows the mountains, the rivers and the temple at the end of the trail. Map Q has the scale 1 cm = 500 m and, along with these, shows symbols for every well, bridge and unmetalled road on the trail. The trail from the base village to the temple measures 3 cm on Map P. The pages of the club's notebook are 20 cm long.
(a) What is the real length of the trail, using Map P?
(b) How long will the same trail be on Map Q?
(c) Why does Map Q have room for wells and bridges that Map P leaves out?
(d) The club wants the whole trail copied onto one notebook page. Which map should it copy, and what will it lose by doing so?
questions.a: (a) 3 x 5 km = 15 km. (b) 15 km = 15,000 m, and 15,000 / 500 = 30 cm. (c) On Map Q each centimetre stands for only 500 m, one-tenth of Map P's 5 km, so the same stretch of ground gets ten times as much length on paper, leaving space for symbols of small features. (d) Map P, because its 3 cm trail fits on the page while Map Q's 30 cm trail is longer than the 20 cm page; but the copy will not show the wells, bridges and unmetalled roads that only Map Q shows.
s: (c) Explains that 1 cm covers less ground on Map Q, so there is more space for symbols
(d) Chooses Map P because 30 cm does not fit a 20 cm page, and names the lost details

questions.q: Which statement best describes the shape of the Earth?
questions.a: It is nearly a sphere, slightly flattened at the poles.
o: It is nearly a sphere, slightly flattened at the poles
It is a perfect sphere with no flattening anywhere
It is nearly a sphere, slightly flattened at the Equator
It is a flat disc with the two poles at its edge

questions.q: A science museum wants one model that shows the land and oceans of the whole Earth without any part being torn or pulled out of shape. Which should it choose?
questions.a: A globe of the Earth, because it has the same spherical shape as the Earth, while a sphere's surface cannot be laid flat on paper without tearing.
o: One large flat map of the world
An atlas with a flat map of each continent
A flat world map with more symbols on it

questions.q:
Read the statements about globes.
I. When a globe is rotated, the two fixed points at its top and bottom are the poles.
II. A globe represents the geography of the Earth better than a flat map, because both have the same spherical shape.
III. A globe may show a map of the Moon or of the planet Mars, not only of the Earth.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I, II and III are all correct.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A flat map cannot represent the whole spherical Earth accurately.
Reason (R): The Earth is slightly flattened at the poles.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A. A flat map fails because the curved surface of a sphere cannot be laid flat without tearing; the slight flattening at the poles is not the cause, and in practice the Earth is treated as a sphere.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: (a) What is a globe? (b) Name two materials a globe is generally made of.
questions.a: (a) A globe is a sphere on which a map is drawn. (b) Any two of metal, plastic and cardboard.
s: (a) A sphere on which a map is drawn
(b) Any two of metal, plastic, cardboard

questions.q: True or False? 'The Earth is not a perfect sphere, yet in practice we treat it as a sphere.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The Earth is slightly flattened at the poles, so it is not a perfect sphere, but the flattening is slight and in practice it is considered to be spherical.
s: Reason: slightly flattened at the poles, but in practice taken as spherical

questions.q: Manoj says, 'A flat world map is just as accurate as a globe, because both are drawn carefully by experts.' (a) Is he right? (b) Give a reason based on the shape of the Earth.
questions.a: (a) No. (b) The Earth is nearly a sphere, and a sphere cannot be represented accurately on a flat sheet however carefully it is drawn; a globe has the same spherical shape as the Earth, so it represents the Earth's geography better.
s: (b) Explains that a sphere cannot be shown accurately on a flat sheet, while a globe shares the Earth's shape

questions.q: (a) A student peels an orange so that the skin comes off in three or four large pieces, and then tries to press them flat on a table. What happens to the pieces? (b) What does this show about drawing the Earth on a flat sheet of paper? (c) Name the object that has the same shape as the Earth and so represents it better.
questions.a: (a) The pieces cannot be flattened without tearing at the edges. (b) A sphere cannot be represented accurately on a flat sheet of paper, so a flat map of the Earth cannot be fully accurate. (c) A globe.
s: (a) They tear at the edges when pressed flat
(b) A sphere cannot be shown accurately on flat paper

questions.q: For an exhibition, Leela paints a world map on a plastic ball. Om prints a world map on a flat sheet of paper and tries to wrap it round a ball of the same size, but the paper crumples, and he has to cut slits in it, leaving gaps. (a) Why could Om's flat sheet not cover the ball neatly? (b) Whose model shows the Earth's geography more accurately, and why? (c) What does Om's problem tell you about any flat map of the whole world?
questions.a: (a) A flat sheet cannot be fitted onto the curved surface of a sphere without folding or tearing, just as orange peel cannot be flattened without tearing. (b) Leela's, because it is a globe: a map drawn on a sphere, the same shape as the Earth. (c) A flat map of the whole world cannot represent the spherical Earth accurately; some parts must be torn apart or pulled out of shape.
s: (a) A flat surface and a sphere's curved surface cannot match without folding or tearing
(b) Leela's model, because it is a globe with the Earth's spherical shape
(c) No flat map of the whole world can be fully accurate

questions.q: Riya writes in her notes: 'The Earth is not a perfect sphere, so a globe is not a true copy of its shape either. So a globe has no advantage over a flat map of the world.' Evaluate her reasoning in four steps: (a) say which part of her first sentence is correct; (b) state how the chapter treats the Earth's shape in practice; (c) explain why a flat map cannot represent a sphere accurately; (d) give your verdict on her conclusion.
questions.a: (a) It is correct that the Earth is not a perfect sphere: it is slightly flattened at the poles. (b) The flattening is slight, so in practice the Earth is considered to be spherical, and a globe matches that shape. (c) The curved surface of a sphere cannot be laid flat without tearing or pulling parts out of shape, as the orange-peel test shows. (d) Her conclusion is wrong: a globe has the same (nearly) spherical shape as the Earth, so it represents the Earth's geography better than a flat map, even if it is not a perfect copy.
s: (a) Agrees the Earth is slightly flattened at the poles
(b) States that in practice the Earth is treated as a sphere
(c) Explains that a sphere's surface cannot be flattened without tearing
(d) Rejects her conclusion: the globe still represents the Earth better

questions.q: What is the latitude of the Equator?
questions.a: 0° (zero degree).

questions.q: A team of scientists works at a station close to the South Pole. Which word from the chapter describes the climate they mostly face?
questions.a: Frigid, the cold climate found close to the North or South Pole.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The parallel of latitude at 70°N is a smaller circle than the parallel at 70°S.
Reason (R): The circles marked by the parallels of latitude grow smaller as we move northward or southward from the Equator.
questions.a: A is false but R is true. Both parallels are 70 degrees from the Equator, one to the north and one to the south, so they shrink by the same amount and are circles of the same size.
o: A is false but R is true.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.

questions.q: Lata says that a town at 13°N and a town at 13°S have the same latitude. Which statement is correct?
questions.a: They are equally far from the Equator but on opposite sides of it, so their latitudes (13°N and 13°S) are different.
o: They are equally far from the Equator but on opposite sides, so their latitudes differ
They have the same latitude, because both are 13 degrees from the Equator
They have the same latitude, because both lie close to the Equator
They are 13 degrees apart, one on each side of the Equator

questions.q: (a) What does latitude measure? (b) Write the latitudes of the North Pole and the South Pole.
questions.a: (a) Latitude measures the distance of a place from the Equator, in degrees, as you travel towards one of the poles. (b) North Pole 90°N; South Pole 90°S.
s: (a) Distance from the Equator towards a pole, in degrees

questions.q: True or False? 'A ship sailing due north from 30°S to 10°S is moving away from the Equator.' Give the verdict and the reason or the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. Its latitude falls from 30° to 10°, and latitude measures distance from the Equator, so the ship is moving closer to the Equator, not away from it.
s: Reason: latitude falls from 30° to 10°, so the ship gets closer to the Equator

questions.q: Ramu tells his friend: 'Meet me at the 3rd stall in the 9th row of the vegetable market.' (a) What two pieces of information does he give? (b) What name does the chapter give to such a system, in which two values fix a place precisely? (c) Name the two values used in this way to fix a place on the Earth.
questions.a: (a) The row (the 9th row) and the stall's place in that row (the 3rd stall). (b) A system of coordinates. (c) Latitude and longitude.
s: (a) The row number and the stall number in the row

questions.q: A weather balloon is released at 25°S and drifts due north through 40 degrees of latitude. (a) At what latitude does it end up? (b) Did it cross the Equator on the way? Explain. (c) At the end, is it nearer to the Equator or farther from it than when it started?
questions.a: (a) It covers 25 degrees to reach the Equator and 15 more beyond it, so it ends at 15°N. (b) Yes: it starts south of the Equator and ends north of it, crossing the Equator after 25 degrees of drift. (c) Nearer: it ends 15 degrees from the Equator, compared with 25 degrees at the start.
s: (b) Yes, it moves from the south side to the north side after 25 degrees
(c) Nearer, since 15 degrees is less than 25 degrees

questions.q:
Three research stations lie at these latitudes: Station A at 2°N, Station B at 45°S and Station C at 78°N.
(a) Which station is nearest to the Equator?
(b) How many degrees of latitude is each station from its nearer pole?
(c) What kind of climate does the link between latitude and climate suggest for Station A, and for Station C?
(d) Of the three parallels on which the stations lie, which is the longest circle and which is the shortest? Give a reason.
(e) Suppose Station B lay due south of Station A. Through how many degrees of latitude would a ship sail going from A to B?
questions.a: (a) Station A, only 2 degrees from the Equator. (b) A: 90 - 2 = 88 degrees from the North Pole; B: 90 - 45 = 45 degrees from the South Pole; C: 90 - 78 = 12 degrees from the North Pole. (c) A: hot (torrid); C: cold (frigid). (d) A's parallel (2°N) is the longest and C's (78°N) the shortest, because parallels grow smaller as they move away from the Equator towards the poles. (e) 2 degrees to reach the Equator plus 45 degrees beyond it = 47 degrees.
s: (d) A's parallel longest, C's shortest, as parallels shrink towards the poles

questions.q:
A geography club in Kochi spins a classroom globe on its stand. Priya marks the two points at the top and the bottom that stay fixed as the globe turns, and then the circle drawn halfway between them. She sticks three paper flags on the globe: Flag 1 on the circle she marked, Flag 2 on the parallel of 40°N and Flag 3 at 90°S. The club notes that Kochi lies close to latitude 10°N.
(a) What are the two fixed points Priya marked called?
(b) What is the circle halfway between them called, and what is its latitude?
(c) Which flag stands on a pole, and which pole is it?
(d) How many degrees of latitude is Kochi from Flag 2?
questions.a: (a) The North Pole and the South Pole. (b) The Equator, latitude 0°. (c) Flag 3, at the South Pole (90°S). (d) 40 - 10 = 30 degrees of latitude.

questions.q: Through which place does the Prime Meridian pass?
questions.a: Greenwich, an area of London in England.
o: Greenwich, an area of London in England

questions.q: Which description fits a meridian of longitude?
questions.a: A half-circle running from one pole to the other.
o: A half-circle running from one pole to the other
A full circle running east and west, parallel to the Equator
A circle that grows smaller towards the poles
A line that always marks the edge of a time zone

questions.q:
Match each position in Column A with the hemispheres it lies in, in Column B.
Column A:
1. 20°N, 40°E
2. 35°S, 60°W
3. 10°S, 120°E
4. 50°N, 100°W
Column B:
A. Southern and Eastern Hemispheres
B. Northern and Western Hemispheres
C. Northern and Eastern Hemispheres
D. Southern and Western Hemispheres

Assertion (A): The longitude 180° is written without the letter E or W.
Reason (R): 180°E and 180°W are the same meridian.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: since 180°W and 180°E are the same longitude, it is noted simply as 180°.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: 'Delhi lies at 29°N latitude and 77°E longitude.' (a) What does 29°N tell you about Delhi's position? (b) What does 77°E tell you?
questions.a: (a) Delhi is 29 degrees north of the Equator. (b) Delhi is 77 degrees east of the Prime Meridian, measured along the Equator.
s: (b) 77 degrees east of the Prime Meridian

questions.q: (a) What was the madhya rekha? (b) Name the famous astronomer who lived and worked about 1,500 years ago in the city it passed through.
questions.a: (a) India's own prime meridian, the 'middle line', which passed through Ujjayini (today Ujjain). (b) Varahamihira.
s: (a) India's ancient prime meridian (middle line) through Ujjayini/Ujjain

questions.q: A sailing chart shows three lighthouses: L1 at 15°S, 45°W; L2 at 30°N, 45°E; L3 at 60°N, 150°W. (a) Which two lighthouses are the same number of degrees of longitude from the Prime Meridian? (b) Which lighthouse lies in both the Northern and the Western Hemispheres? (c) How many degrees of longitude apart are L1 and L2, measured across the Prime Meridian?
questions.a: (a) L1 and L2, both 45 degrees from the Prime Meridian (one west, one east). (b) L3 (60°N, 150°W). (c) 45 + 45 = 90 degrees of longitude.
s: (c) 90 degrees, adding the two sides of the Prime Meridian

questions.q: An island lies at 20°S, 60°E. In four steps, explain how these two coordinates fix its position: (a) what 20°S tells you; (b) what 60°E tells you; (c) in which two hemispheres the island lies; (d) why giving only 20°S would not be enough to find the island.
questions.a: (a) The island is 20 degrees south of the Equator. (b) It is 60 degrees east of the Prime Meridian, measured along the Equator. (c) The Southern Hemisphere (south of the Equator) and the Eastern Hemisphere (east of the Prime Meridian). (d) 20°S is a parallel, a circle running all the way round the Earth, and every place on it has latitude 20°S; the longitude 60°E picks out one point on that circle, just as a row number alone does not find a shop without its place in the row.
s: (b) 60 degrees east of the Prime Meridian
(d) A parallel circles the Earth, so the longitude is needed to fix one point

questions.a: (a) Parallels run east and west, parallel to the Equator; meridians run from one pole to the other (north to south). (b) Parallels are full circles around the Earth; meridians are half-circles. (c) Parallels grow smaller as they move from the Equator towards the poles; meridians are all the same length, since every shortest route from pole to pole covers the same distance. (d) The Equator is 0° latitude; the Prime Meridian (Greenwich) is 0° longitude. (e) Latitude goes up to 90°, as 90°N or 90°S at the poles; longitude goes up to 180°, written E or W, except that 180° itself needs no letter.
s: (a) East-west for parallels, pole to pole for meridians
(c) Parallels shrink towards the poles; meridians are all equal

questions.q:
A coastguard centre receives distress calls from three fishing boats: Boat X at 5°S, 80°E; Boat Y at 12°N, 72°E; Boat Z at 5°S, 95°E. Its rescue ship is at 5°S, 70°E. The ship is told to help the boats on its own parallel first, and it can sail only along that parallel, eastward or westward.
(a) Which boat is in the Northern Hemisphere?
(b) Which boats lie on the same parallel as the rescue ship?
(c) How many degrees of longitude is the ship from Boat X, and from Boat Z?
(d) Which of these two boats should the ship reach first so that it never has to turn back? Justify using their longitudes.
questions.a: (a) Boat Y, because 12°N is north of the Equator. (b) Boats X and Z, which are both at 5°S like the ship. (c) X: 80 - 70 = 10 degrees; Z: 95 - 70 = 25 degrees. (d) Boat X first. Both boats lie east of the ship, and X (80°E) comes before Z (95°E), so the ship sails 10 degrees east to X and then 15 more to Z, 25 degrees in all with no turning back; going to Z first would mean 25 degrees out and 15 degrees back west to X, 40 degrees in all.
s: (d) Chooses Boat X first and compares 25 degrees with 40 degrees

questions.q: By how much is Indian Standard Time (IST) ahead of Greenwich Mean Time (GMT)?
questions.a: 5 hours 30 minutes.

questions.q: When it is 12 noon at Greenwich, what is the local time at 60°E?
questions.a: 4 pm: 60 degrees east is 60 / 15 = 4 hours ahead.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Indian Standard Time is ahead of Greenwich Mean Time.
Reason (R): India lies to the west of the Prime Meridian.
questions.a: A is true but R is false. IST is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT, but India's longitudes (about 68°E to 97°E) lie east of the Prime Meridian, which is why its time is ahead.
o: A is true but R is false.
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: A news bulletin is heard at 6 pm local time in a town at 45°E. What is the local time at that moment in a town at 30°W?
questions.a: 1 pm: the towns are 45 + 30 = 75 degrees apart, which is 5 hours, and the western town is behind.

questions.q: (a) What is standard time? (b) Why do most countries use a standard time instead of the local time of each place?
questions.a: (a) Standard time is one time adopted by a whole country, based on a meridian passing through it. (b) It would not be convenient for a country to use many different local times.
s: (a) One time for the country, based on a meridian passing through it
(b) Using many local times would be inconvenient

questions.q: True or False? 'A town at 30°N, 45°E and a town at 20°S, 45°E have the same local time.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Local time depends on longitude, changing by one hour for every 15 degrees east or west; both towns are at 45°E, so their local time is the same even though their latitudes differ.
s: Reason: local time depends on longitude, and both towns share 45°E

questions.q: (a) Two places are 45 degrees of longitude apart. What is the difference in their local times? (b) If the eastern place shows 9 am local time, what local time does the western place show?
questions.a: (a) 45 / 15 = 3 hours. (b) The western place is 3 hours behind, so it shows 6 am.

questions.q: Sahil lives in a town in Arunachal Pradesh, in the far east of India, and his cousin lives in a town in Gujarat, in the far west. Sahil says: 'Our watches both show 6:00 pm right now, so the local time must be the same in both towns.' (a) Why do both watches show the same time? (b) Which town's local time is ahead, and why? (c) Is Sahil right? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Both watches follow Indian Standard Time, the one standard time used across the whole country. (b) The town in Arunachal Pradesh, because it lies farther east, and local time increases as you go east (one hour for every 15 degrees). (c) No. The watches show the same standard time, but the local times of the two towns are different; this is why the sun can set in the east of India while it is still daylight in the west.
s: (a) Both follow IST, a single standard time
(b) The eastern town, because local time increases eastward
(c) No: same standard time, different local times

questions.q:
A school in Chennai plans a live online class with a partner school in a town on the Prime Meridian that keeps GMT. The Chennai school is open from 8:00 am to 2:00 pm IST. The partner school is open from 8:00 am to 3:00 pm GMT. The class will last 1 hour 45 minutes. IST is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT.
(a) When the partner school opens at 8:00 am GMT, what time is it in Chennai?
(b) When the Chennai school closes at 2:00 pm IST, what time is it at the partner school?
(c) For how long are both schools open at the same time?
(d) Can the whole class fit inside the hours when both schools are open? Explain.
(e) If the class starts the moment the partner school opens, how long must the Chennai school stay open after its usual closing time?
questions.a: (a) 8:00 am + 5 h 30 min = 1:30 pm IST. (b) 2:00 pm - 5 h 30 min = 8:30 am GMT. (c) From 1:30 pm to 2:00 pm IST, that is 30 minutes. (d) No: the class needs 1 hour 45 minutes, but the two schools are open together for only 30 minutes. (e) The class runs from 1:30 pm to 3:15 pm IST, so Chennai must stay open 1 hour 15 minutes after 2:00 pm.
s: (d) No, 30 minutes is less than 1 hour 45 minutes

questions.q:
Four radio stations go on air at the same instant, and each announces its own local time. Station P is in a town on the Prime Meridian that keeps GMT; Station Q is at 30°E; Station R is at 45°W; Station S is at 90°E. At that instant Station P announces '10:00 am'. Local time changes by one hour for every 15 degrees of longitude.
(a) What local time does Station Q announce?
(b) What local time does Station R announce?
(c) What local time does Station S announce?
(d) A listener in India hears Station S. Should she set her watch to the time S announces? What should her watch show?
questions.a: (a) 30 / 15 = 2 hours ahead: 12:00 noon. (b) 45 / 15 = 3 hours behind: 7:00 am. (c) 90 / 15 = 6 hours ahead: 4:00 pm. (d) No. India follows Indian Standard Time, 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT, so her watch should show 3:30 pm; S's local time is 30 minutes ahead of IST.
s: (d) No; IST is 3:30 pm, so she keeps standard time, not S's local time

questions.q: According to the chapter, how many time zones does Russia have?
questions.a: 11 time zones.

questions.q: At approximately which longitude does the International Date Line lie?
questions.a: About 180°, opposite the Prime Meridian.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A traveller crossing Russia from east to west must readjust her watch 10 times to keep up with the local time.
Reason (R): Russia has 11 time zones.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: passing through 11 zones means crossing 10 zone boundaries, and the watch is readjusted at each one.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
Read the statements.
I. The USA has six time zones.
II. A ship crossing the International Date Line westward on a Sunday changes its date to Saturday.
III. The lines dividing time zones are not fully straight because they tend to follow international borders.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: crossing the Date Line westward adds a day, so Sunday becomes Monday.

questions.q: A ship crosses the International Date Line travelling westward on a Tuesday. (a) Must the crew add a day or subtract a day? (b) Which day will the new date fall on?
questions.a: (a) Add a day, because the line is crossed westward. (b) Wednesday.

questions.q: True or False? 'The International Date Line is a perfectly straight line along 180° longitude.' Give the verdict and the corrected statement.
questions.a: False. The International Date Line lies only approximately at 180°; it deviates in places to avoid dividing some countries into two different days.
s: Corrects it: it is only approximately at 180° and bends to avoid splitting countries into two days

questions.q: (a) Why are the lines dividing the time zones on a world map not fully straight? (b) Name two countries that the chapter says are too large to have a single time zone. (c) On the time-zone map, a country is marked '+3'. What does this number mean?
questions.a: (a) They have to respect each country's standard time, so they tend to follow international borders. (b) Any two of Russia, Canada and the USA. (c) Its standard time is found by adding 3 hours to GMT.
s: (a) They follow international borders to respect each country's standard time
(b) Any two of Russia, Canada, the USA
(c) Add 3 hours to GMT to get its standard time

questions.q: Maya's ship crosses the International Date Line westward on a Saturday morning. That same evening the ship turns round and crosses the line again, this time eastward. Maya says, 'By the end of the day I will have lost a whole day.' (a) What does the date become after the first crossing? (b) What does it become after the second crossing? (c) Is Maya right? Explain.
questions.a: (a) Crossing westward adds a day, so Saturday becomes Sunday. (b) Crossing eastward subtracts a day, so Sunday goes back to Saturday. (c) No. The two changes cancel each other, so she has neither lost nor gained a day; she is back on Saturday.
s: (c) No: the two changes cancel out

questions.q: A sports channel shows a world map of standard times. Country A is marked +3, Country B is marked -5 and Country C is marked +9. India keeps IST, which is 5 hours 30 minutes ahead of GMT. (a) When it is 12 noon GMT, what time is it in Country A? (b) At that same moment, what time is it in Country B? (c) By how much is Country C's standard time ahead of IST? (d) A final in Country C begins at 8:00 pm local time. Can a student in India watch it live from the start before her 10:00 pm bedtime? Show the time.
questions.a: (a) 12 noon + 3 hours = 3:00 pm. (b) 12 noon - 5 hours = 7:00 am. (c) 9 hours - 5 hours 30 minutes = 3 hours 30 minutes. (d) Yes. 8:00 pm in Country C is 8:00 pm - 3 h 30 min = 4:30 pm IST, well before 10:00 pm.
s: (d) Converts to 4:30 pm IST and says yes

questions.q:
A plane leaves a city in the +11 time zone at 11:00 pm on Friday, local time. It flies eastward for 5 hours, crossing the International Date Line, and lands in a city in the -10 time zone.
(a) What are the GMT time and day when the plane leaves?
(b) What are the GMT time and day when it lands?
(c) What are the local time and day in the -10 city when it lands?
(d) Using the rule for crossing the Date Line, explain why the day shown at landing is not Saturday.
(e) A passenger says, 'I landed before I took off, so I travelled back in time.' Evaluate her claim.
questions.a: (a) 11:00 pm Friday - 11 hours = 12:00 noon on Friday, GMT. (b) 12:00 noon + 5 hours = 5:00 pm Friday GMT. (c) 5:00 pm - 10 hours = 7:00 am on Friday. (d) In the +11 city's time the plane lands at 4:00 am on Saturday, but it has crossed the Date Line eastward, and crossing eastward subtracts a day, so the date goes back to Friday. (e) Her claim is wrong: the flight really took 5 hours; only the clock readings and the date changed because the two cities keep standard times 21 hours apart.
s: (d) Eastward crossing subtracts a day, so Saturday goes back to Friday
(e) Rejects the claim: 5 hours passed; only clocks and date differ (21-hour gap)
